newsitem.title: USA: Airlines reexamine hedging after fuel price surge.
newsitem.headline: Airlines reexamine hedging after fuel price surge.

text.p: A surge in jet fuel costs over the past couple of months left some U.S. airlines more exposed than others and stirred up renewed interest in hedging among the major carriers.
The U.S.-Iraq face-off in the Gulf and sinking domestic inventories combined to push New York Harbor jet fuel prices up nearly 40 pct since the mid-summer trough to more than 72 cents a gallon.
With airline load factors expected to increase in the months ahead, jet traders see further price pressure on jet, which typically accounts for 10 to 15 percent of a carrier's costs.

A move by Continental Airlines to hedge a significant portion of its fuel costs into 1997 could prove a milestone for airlines in terms of hedging, said Candace Browning, airline industry analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co.
"KLM (Royal Dutch Airlines) did hedge a considerable amount before but nobody's ever hedged 100 pct," as Continental has into early 1997, said Browning.

"(Airlines) think that over a long period of time they are as likely to lose money on a hedge as make money so they've been reluctant. But that is being reassessed at many airlines right now," she added.
Continental's aggressive strategy, which reportedly fixes their fuel cost at about 20 pct below current market prices, has proved a winner.

"We are hedged through to the end of next year to a certain extent but a lot of (airlines) are not. I don't know what I'd do if I wasn't -- it is a little scary out there," said Rick Pressley, director of fuels management at Continental.
"It sems to be an industry that is not too comfortable with hedging but it is certainly going to get a lot of attention now," Pressley added.
Among the major U.S. carriers the resistance towards managing their fuel price risk has been breaking down, but only slowly.
"Historically, you haven't seen much hedging in the U.S. industry, not nearly as much as some of the overseas carriers," said Jeff Long, airline analyst at J.P. Morgan.

"Delta went in last year with a kind of deviation-against-the-mean programme and Continental this year with their more aggressive one. People are edging in that direction and seeing that fuel is a risk they shouldn't be totally exposed to," Long said.

Airlines looking to hedge their exposure to jet fuel costs mostly have confined their efforts to the New York Mercantile Exchange, where the heating oil futures contract generally tracks jet fuel prices. However, that can prove a very risky strategy when jet and heating oil prices diverge, as happened dramatically during the Gulf War and, to a lesser extent, several times since, most recently last spring.
Though tailor-made options and swaps traded on an over-the-counter basis can eliminate that risk, those markets are sometimes illiquid and difficult to get in and out of quickly.
But jet fuel hedging markets "have gotten a lot more visibility (in the airline industry) since the Gulf War," said Long of J.P. Morgan.

"Their is an increasing level of concern about fuel fuel prices over the years and when you start to get carriers making more aggressive moves, like Continental, it removes one obstacle to using the markets, which is that nobody wants to be out there on their own in case it goes wrong," Long said.
